title: Panaetius softens the porch
hookLine: Panaetius brought Stoicism to Rome and made it more humane for ordinary people

lines: A CHAMPION'S PHOTO, OR "YOU SHOWED UP"?
cards: Some gyms post a photo of a champion by the door: this is the goal. Others post a sign: you showed up, that counts. Both want you stronger.

Only one makes a beginner want to come back. The early Stoics talked a lot about the sage, the perfectly wise person, and admitted that almost nobody had ever been one. That's a hard poster to walk past every day.
Then a philosopher from the island of Rhodes carried the school to Rome and quietly changed the sign on the door. Today: kathēkon.

teach.b: First, the man. Panaetius of Rhodes spent years in Rome among the circle of Scipio Aemilianus, a leading general and statesman, and later became head of the Stoic school in Athens.
Later writers credit him with helping Stoicism take root in Rome. Second, the change. Earlier Stoics drew a sharp line: the sage is wise, everyone else is a fool, and there's nothing in between.
Panaetius, as later writers report him, cared about the people in between, those making progress.
He wrote about duties for ordinary life: how a decent person acts as a citizen, a friend, a family member, in their own particular role. Third, the word.
His book was called On Appropriate Action; the Greek is kathēkon, what's fitting for you to do. Cicero later rebuilt it into a Latin book, On Duties, coming up in a few days.
And Panaetius taught that each person has their own nature, too: not everyone should try to live the same life. Fourth, why it mattered. He didn't throw out the high ideal.

teach.h: A PATH ORDINARY PEOPLE COULD WALK.
teach.b: He made a path toward it that ordinary people could walk.
A senator, a soldier, a parent could do the fitting thing today without being a sage.
Looking back over the week: Zeno's vision, Cleanthes' praise, Chrysippus's structure, and now Panaetius, making a door more people could walk through.

how: Historians of philosophy describe Panaetius as the Stoic who turned the school's attention to people making progress and to fitting duties in ordinary roles, an approach later passed on through Cicero.

o: the fitting action, what's right for you to do
a strict rule that's the same for everyone
the perfect wisdom only a sage can reach

s: Panaetius threw out the Stoic ideal of the sage
he kept the ideal but wrote for those still on the way to it.
Cicero's On Duties was built on Panaetius's book
Cicero reworked Panaetius's work on fitting action into Latin.
Panaetius taught that every person should live exactly the same life
he taught that each has their own nature, and their own fitting path.

games.q: you lead a demanding school whose ideal almost nobody reaches. Romans are curious but busy. what do you write?
o: a book on fitting duties for people making progress.
nothing; let only the dedicated in.
games.why: Panaetius wrote on appropriate action for ordinary roles, a gentler door into the school, and Rome walked through it.

practice: Think of one practice you keep failing at because the bar is set too high: twenty minutes of meditation, never getting angry, reading every day.
Size it, the Panaetius way, for a real person in your real life: twenty minutes becomes two, never angry becomes one pause. Let your shoulders drop as you choose the gentler version.

wordCard.voice: Kathēkon. Panaetius's word for the fitting action, what's appropriate for you to do; Cicero later translated it as duty. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: what's fitting, the appropriate action. Panaetius's subject; Cicero translated it into Latin as officium, duty.

carryVoice: Your line: gentler for everyone. The high ideal stays; the door just gets wider. That's a week, from Marcus to the porch.

sources.work: Diogenes Laërtius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers
